title: Finding a stylist, trichologist or dermatologist who knows afro hair
question_forms: Who should I see about hair loss or a scalp problem: a GP, dermatologist or trichologist?
tradition_says: Word of mouth is the way: ask someone with hair like yours. For hair loss, a trusted stylist is often seen first, and doctors are thought not to know afro hair.

layer1.plain_answer: A stylist or loctician is the right person for styling and a trichologist or dermatologist for hair loss. In the UK a GP can refer you to a dermatologist; trichologists are not medically qualified, so check that they are registered and have experience with afro-textured hair. Ask directly what share of their patients have hair like yours.

do.text: Ask a doctor for a referral to a dermatologist if hair loss or scalp symptoms persist.
See a board-certified dermatologist if you notice texture change or even slight thinning.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care"

do.text: Use the Institute of Trichologists register and ask about experience with afro-textured hair; its page does not mention afro hair or say members are medically qualified.

source.name: Institute of Trichologists (professional association; its register is accredited by the Professional Standards Authority; the page does not say members are medically qualified and does not mention afro hair)

do.text: Have braids, relaxers and locs done by a trained professional.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Caring for Afro-textured hair" (July 2023)

do.text: Ask a loctician or braider to loosen anything that hurts: pain equals damage.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Black hair: tips for everyday care"

avoid.text: Waiting on thinning at the crown or hairline because a stylist says it is just breakage.

source.name: British Association of Dermatologists, patient leaflet "Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia"

avoid.text: Assuming a clinician will recognise your hair condition: CCCA is underrecognised and often misdiagnosed.

see_someone_when: Hair is thinning at the crown, hairline or part (dermatologist).
A shiny, smooth scalp with no hair openings (dermatologist soon).

tested.finding: CCCA mostly presents as progressive thinning of the central scalp, may resemble androgenetic alopecia or alopecia areata, and is underrecognised and often misdiagnosed. Dermoscopy and biopsy remain important.

tested.design: PubMed search run 12 Nov 2026, exact string: (afro-textured hair OR "ethnic hair" OR "hair disorders") AND (dermatology residency OR "dermatology training" OR curriculum OR "residency programs") (result count 36).
tested.finding: My search found nothing relevant: the string returned 36 results: I read the first 12 titles (of 36, newest first): none is a UK audit or directory. US papers on training exist, for example resident comfort treating hair conditions in patients with skin of colour (PMID 38873622) and a call for ethnic hair education (PMID 39822984); I read titles only. This question is partly not a PubMed question: the British Association of Dermatologists directory was not opened. Control: PubMed search "Khumalo NP AND hair" returned 71 results on the same day. Earlier note kept: My search found nothing: no directory or training audit of UK clinicians for afro hair found; I did not open the British Association of Dermatologists directory in this pass.

tier_driver: That a particular type of practitioner (a trichologist, a Black clinician, a loctician) gives better outcomes: no study found.
tier_note: D because the claim (a specialist who knows afro hair gets better results) has no outcome study; CCCA under-recognition is a B line. A study of outcomes by practitioner type would move it.
harm_note: No harm signal found. A trichologist is not medically qualified (the Institute's page does not say members are), so a scarring condition needs a dermatologist.
evidence_summary: A 2026 review says CCCA is underrecognised and often misdiagnosed because it overlaps with other hair loss (Persson). The Institute of Trichologists runs an accredited register (PSA scheme) and a Level 5 course; its page does not mention afro hair or say members are medically qualified. The AAD says see a dermatologist for texture change or slight thinning. There are no published outcome data by practitioner type, and I did not find a UK directory of clinicians with afro hair expertise.
measured_variables: Practitioner experience with afro-textured hair (not measured)
gaps: Untested: outcomes by practitioner; a reliable UK directory of dermatologists with afro hair training; how to judge a loctician or braider for scalp safety. 12 Nov: choosing a stylist, braider or loctician (styling, not medical) now has its own entry, choosing-a-stylist-braider-or-loctician.
